claims.text: The starting nanoparticles are equiatomic Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu.
The starting Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are nominally a single-phase solid solution.
The constituent metals have different cohesive energies, with Cu having a relatively low cohesive contribution.
Cohesive-energy differences drive selective surface segregation in equiatomic Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles at elevated temperature.
Cu preferentially migrates toward the nanoparticle surface because Cu-containing metallic bonds are comparatively less cohesive.
Selective segregation creates a core-shell compositional gradient with a Cu-enriched surface.
A compositionally distinct surface layer triggers premelting at the surface before the particle interior disorders.
Premelting progresses from the nanoparticle surface inward.
Slow cooling provides more time for atomic diffusion than rapid cooling.
Additional diffusion during slow cooling enhances surface segregation and surface-layer formation.
Rapidly cooled Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles retain a relatively homogeneous single-phase elemental distribution with minimal surface segregation.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles will show a more pronounced radial compositional gradient and greater Cu surface enrichment than rapidly cooled nanoparticles.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles will exhibit surface premelting at a lower temperature than rapidly cooled nanoparticles.
Surface segregation changes the melting pathway relative to that of uniformly quenched nanoparticles.
The relevant premelting and melting regime for these nanoparticles lies within 600–1400 °C.
Oxidation or competing phase transformations may prevent the proposed segregation-controlled mechanism from applying.
The mechanism may not transfer to high-entropy alloys with significantly different compositions.
Atomistic modeling of an HEA nanoparticle found little long-range chemical ordering but some short-range ordering.
Short-range ordering may moderate the extent of surface segregation in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles.

contradictions.description: Cooling is described as occurring after heating and as controlling post-heating atomic reordering, yet the predicted comparison is an earlier premelting onset during heating. A subsequent cooling rate cannot alter an onset temperature already observed on the preceding heating ramp unless a cooling-and-reheating cycle is explicitly introduced.
